title: What each approach does well, and what it misses
source: My reading of each approach’s published methods: Pew Research Center, Gallup and YouGov methodology statements, AI Impacts (2024), the Forecasting Research Institute (2023 and 2026), Anthropic’s 81k methods appendix (2026), the Computational Democracy Project, the Collective Intelligence Project, the neoneye P(doom) calculator’s reports, Moreira et al. (2025) and Doom or Bloom’s about page.
hint: Hover, tap or focus a mark to see why it scores that way

columns.label: Sample
columns.detail: Does it reach people who stand for a wider population, rather than whoever shows up?

columns.label: Wording
columns.detail: Does everyone get the same neutral questions, in an order that doesn’t lead?

columns.label: Reasons
columns.detail: Can people say why, in their own words?

columns.label: Gives back
columns.detail: Does each person get something back for their time?

columns.label: Checks
columns.detail: When someone or something interprets the answers, can people see and correct the reading?

columns.label: Openness
columns.detail: Are the exact wording, the methods and the data public?

columns.label: Over time
columns.detail: Is it repeated with the same questions, so change shows up?

columns.label: Languages
columns.detail: Can people take part in their own language?

sample.note: Pew and Gallup recruit panels by mail or phone and weight them to the census; YouGov weights an opt-in online panel

wording.note: The same fixed wording for everyone, with answer options rotated to spread order effects

reasons.note: Mostly closed questions; Pew sometimes adds open-ended follow-ups

gives-back.note: Nothing personal; the public gets the toplines

open.note: Toplines print the exact wording, sample sizes and methods

over-time.note: Pew has asked the same concern question since 2021, Gallup its harm-or-good question since 2023

languages.note: Most polls cover one country; Pew’s global survey asks the same question in dozens

sample.note: A defined group, such as authors at top AI venues, but about one in ten answers and researchers at AI companies are underweighted

wording.note: Exact wording is published, and AI Impacts assigns wording variants at random to measure their effect

reasons.note: Mostly numbers; the forecasting tournament also had participants argue their cases in writing

gives-back.note: Payment or a donation for researchers’ time; no personal result

open.note: Full questions, methods and results are published with each report

over-time.note: AI Impacts asked in 2016, 2022, 2023 and 2024; FRI’s panel reports wave after wave

sample.note: Claude users who chose to take part; Anthropic checked the mix against its own users, not the public

wording.note: Four fixed core questions, with follow-ups Claude writes. Hopes came before concerns, which Anthropic notes could prime answers

reasons.note: Long answers in people’s own words

gives-back.note: A closing recap and, later, the published findings; the 2026 study lets people publish their interview

checks.note: Classifiers code the transcripts afterwards, each checked against one human on 25 labels; participants don’t see their coding

open.note: A methods appendix with two classifier prompts and selected quotes; full interviews only from the 2026 study, by choice

over-time.note: Several studies on one tool, each asking different questions

rows.label: Deliberation platforms
rows.detail: Polis, Global Dialogues, Collective Constitutional AI

sample.note: Global Dialogues and Collective Constitutional AI recruit to quotas, and Global Dialogues reports how representative most rounds were; open Polis conversations take whoever comes

wording.note: Organizers set the prompt; participants write most of the statements everyone votes on

gives-back.note: You see the opinion groups and where you sit, not a personal result

checks.note: Votes, not an interpreter, decide which statements rise; machine summaries are newer and less tested

open.note: Polis is open source; Collective Constitutional AI released its votes and analysis; Global Dialogues publishes its data and code

over-time.note: Global Dialogues repeats a core of questions every round; most Polis conversations run once

languages.note: Global Dialogues runs in several languages; most Polis conversations in one

wording.note: Fixed steps, but each calculator picks the steps, and suggested starting values stick: on one, 36% of quiz-takers kept the number it proposed

gives-back.note: A number of your own, instantly

open.note: One publishes every submission; most publish nothing

rows.label: The Hall of AI Fears and Hopes

sample.note: 330 Americans from an online panel, sampled to match the census

reasons.note: People wrote out their fears and hopes

gives-back.note: A portrait among TIME’s 100 most influential people in AI, next to the three most like you

checks.note: The placement is computed; the paper describes no way to check or change it

open.note: Methods and results in an open paper

sample.note: Whoever chooses to take it; so far mostly two launch-week crowds, from Hacker News and from X

wording.note: Everyone starts with the same open question and draws on the same authored questions, but the order adapts to each person

reasons.note: Every answer is in your own words

gives-back.note: A place on the map, a P(doom) and the simulated thought leaders closest to you

checks.note: You place yourself before seeing the result, can trace each reading back to your answers and say whether it feels right; not yet checked against human coders

open.note: The questions and code are public; data only as aggregates of 10 or more people, and conversations people choose to publish

over-time.note: Runs continuously, with each result tied to a version of the engine, but only since September 2026
